title: Disinfection and Sterilization

unit.title: Clinical Office Practice and Patient Safety

sections.learningObjectives:
- Distinguish high-level disinfection from sterilization, including what each process does and does not accomplish.
- Describe the methods of sterilization used in ambulatory settings, with emphasis on steam (autoclave) principles and limitations.
- Apply the Spaulding classification to determine whether a given item requires cleaning, disinfection, high-level disinfection, or sterilization.
- Explain how sterilization is monitored using mechanical, chemical, and biological indicators, and the appropriate response to failures.
- Recognize the medical office assistant's role in reprocessing and monitoring, including following manufacturer instructions, facility policy, and escalating problems.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Sterilization is like making something completely germ-free, so even the toughest seed-like germs (spores) are destroyed.

### Question 2

High-level disinfection cleans so thoroughly that almost every germ is killed, leaving only the hardest-to-kill seed-like germs behind.

### Question 3

Spores are like seeds with a tough coat; only the very strongest cleaning (sterilization) can be sure to destroy them.

### Question 4

Think of a ladder: wipe dirt off, kill some germs, kill almost all germs, then kill every last germ.

### Question 5

Anything going inside the body where it is normally germ-free has to be completely germ-free first.

### Question 6

Surfaces like the inside of your mouth are sensitive, so instruments touching them must be almost germ-free, even if not fully sterile.

### Question 7

Things that only touch unbroken skin are like your own tabletop; a good wipe-down is usually enough.

### Question 8

Inside the body there are no defenses like skin, so we need a perfect germ-kill to keep patients safe.

### Question 9

A moist lining like the inside of your nose is tougher than the deep inside of your body, so it is okay if a few tough spores are left behind.

### Question 10

If a tool cannot be safely sterilized the usual way, we swap it for a pre-sterilized throwaway tool rather than risk an infection.

### Question 11

A quick wipe is not enough for something going near a sensitive body lining; it needs the extra-strong treatment.

### Question 12

Some special liquids are strong enough to kill almost every germ and are used when heat would ruin an instrument.

### Question 13

After a strong chemical bath, we wash the leftover chemical off with clean water so the tool is safe and stays clean.

### Question 14

Sterilization is all germs gone, while high-level disinfection is almost all germs gone.

### Question 15

Just like a stain remover needs time to work, the germ-killing liquid must soak the tool for the full recommended time.

### Question 16

Strong germ-killer liquids can wipe out even the extra-tough tuberculosis germ, but still not every seed-like spore.

### Question 17

An autoclave is like a super-hot pressure cooker that blasts tools with steam to kill every germ.

### Question 18

Squeezing the steam raises the heat, and hotter steam is better at killing germs deep inside packages.

### Question 19

The autoclave cooks steam at 250 degrees Fahrenheit, far hotter than boiling water, to kill germs.

### Question 20

Turn the heat up and germs die faster; that is why some cycles use an even hotter setting for a shorter time.

### Question 21

Steam is a favorite because it is quick, cheap, and safe, as long as the tool can handle the heat and wetness.

### Question 22

If a plastic tool would melt in a hot steamer, we do not put it in; we use a gentler method instead.

### Question 23

Wash and dry the tools first so the steam can reach every nook and cranny.

### Question 24

A dry-heat oven is like a very hot oven that bakes germs away without any steam.

### Question 25

Without steam to help, the oven has to be even hotter to kill germs.

### Question 26

Things like oils and powders do not like water, so we sterilize them with dry heat instead of steam.

### Question 27

Ethylene oxide is a special gas that kills germs without using heat, so it is good for delicate tools.

### Question 28

After gas cleaning, items sit and air out so no harmful gas is left on them.

### Question 29

This gas is strong medicine for germs but can also hurt people, so it is used only with careful safety rules.

### Question 30

Hydrogen peroxide gas is another gentle, low-heat way to sterilize delicate tools.

### Question 31

Some tools cannot take heat, so we soak them in an extra-strong liquid for a long time instead.

### Question 32

You cannot kill germs hiding under a layer of dirt; clean first so the germ-killer can reach them.

### Question 33

Leave scissors open so the steam can get into the hinge where germs hide.

### Question 34

The wrapper is like a filter: steam gets in to clean, but germs cannot get in afterward.

### Question 35

If the steamer is jam-packed, the steam cannot reach every tool; leave room for it to flow.

### Question 36

Stand the pouches up like books on a shelf so steam flows around each one.

### Question 37

A germ can hide on just one tiny spot, so every single surface must meet the hot steam.

### Question 38

If a package comes out damp, germs can sneak in through the wetness, so we cannot trust it.

### Question 39

A damp package is like an open door for germs; we do not use it, we clean it again.

### Question 40

Sometimes a tool is needed right now, so it is quickly steamed and used immediately, but only for urgent moments.

### Question 41

The careful, packaged way is safer; the right-now way skips steps, so we save it for true emergencies.

### Question 42

Without its wrapper, a freshly cleaned tool can pick up germs on the way to the doctor.

### Question 43

A little oil keeps metal tools from rusting so they last and stay safe to use.

### Question 44

The wrapper has to match the cleaning method, like choosing the right lid for a jar.

### Question 45

Some tools are meant to be thrown away after one use; trying to clean and reuse them is not safe.

### Question 46

Different cleaners need different kinds of wrapping so the cleaning can actually get through.

### Question 47

The rulebook for each tool tells you exactly how to clean it; always check the instructions.

### Question 48

Tools used in surgery go inside the body, so they must be completely germ-free.

### Question 49

A speculum touches sensitive internal lining, so it needs the strong, almost-sterile cleaning.

### Question 50

A cuff only touches unbroken skin, so a good wipe-down is enough.

### Question 51

Wipe the stethoscope between patients to stop germs from hitching a ride.

### Question 52

Needles are used once on one person and then thrown away, never reused.

### Question 53

Things going into the bladder must be germ-free, since the bladder has no germ defense.

### Question 54

A tool that cuts into the body must be perfectly germ-free.

### Question 55

Because it goes near the throat lining, the blade needs the strong, almost-sterile cleaning.

### Question 56

For something permanently placed in the body, we double-check with a special spore test before using it.

### Question 57

Equipment that goes near the lungs' lining needs the strong, almost-sterile cleaning.

### Question 58

The eye is very sensitive, so instruments that touch it need the strong germ-killing treatment.

### Question 59

Blood can carry germs, so wear gloves, wash it all off, and then clean the tool properly.

### Question 60

First wash, then check, then wrap, then steam, then store safely.

### Question 61

One-use items get thrown away after one use; no saving and re-cleaning them.

### Question 62

The Spaulding rule sorts items into three baskets (body-deep, lining, or skin) to decide how clean they must be.

### Question 63

When you are not sure how clean something must be, ask the boss and read the instructions; do not guess.

### Question 64

A tool that only taps unbroken skin just needs a good wipe-down.

### Question 65

Fast-spinning tools can hide germs inside, so they need the full sterilization treatment, not just a wipe.

### Question 66

A tool that goes into a germ-free space inside the body still has to be germ-free, even if it cannot handle the steamer.

### Question 67

We check the machine's work to be sure every germ really was killed.

### Question 68

Watching the gauges to make sure the machine reached the right heat and pressure is like checking a timer on an oven.

### Question 69

The tape changes color to show the package went through the machine; it is like a ticket stub, not a germ test.

### Question 70

A little strip inside the pack tells us the steam actually got all the way inside.

### Question 71

The color strip says the heat got here, but only a spore test proves every germ is dead.

### Question 72

A spore test puts the toughest germs through the machine; if they die, everything else died too.

### Question 73

If the machine can kill the toughest seed-like germs, it can definitely kill the weaker ones.

### Question 74

Each kind of cleaning machine has its own special test germ; steam uses a heat-loving one.

### Question 75

Dry-heat and gas machines use a different test germ than the steam machine.

### Question 76

The spore test is the strongest proof that the machine really killed everything.

### Question 77

The machine gets its spore test at least once a week, and every time it cleans an implant.

### Question 78

For something that stays in the body, we run the spore test and wait for the all-clear before using it.

### Question 79

If the spore test fails, we pull back the tools, fix the machine, and re-clean everything.

### Question 80

Negative is actually good news here; it means the test germs all died.

### Question 81

This special test makes sure no trapped air is blocking the steam from doing its job.

### Question 82

An integrator is a smarter color strip that checks more than one thing at once.

### Question 83

It is like checking the oven temperature, the timer, and tasting the food; each check tells you something different.

### Question 84

Writing down each load is like keeping a receipt; if there is ever a problem, you can look back and find it.

### Question 85

Label each package like a food container; when it was made and what is inside.

### Question 86

A sealed, dry package stays safe until something damages it, like a sealed snack bag.

### Question 87

A torn package is like a broken seal on food; do not use it, clean it again.

### Question 88

If the color strip did not change, do not trust the package; run it through again.

### Question 89

Your job is to follow the checklist, write down the results, and tell the boss right away if something looks wrong.

### Question 90

Keeping notes is how we prove everything was done right and can find any package if there is ever a problem.
